reviewQuestions.question: Why must the same analyzer run at index time and query time?
reviewQuestions.answer: Search matches tokens, not raw text. If indexing lowercases and stems but the query does not, the query token will never equal the indexed token, so the document is unfindable.

reviewQuestions.question: How does an inverted index differ from a forward index, and why is it faster for search?
reviewQuestions.answer: A forward index maps doc → terms; an inverted index maps term → docs (postings). Search asks 'which docs contain this term', which the inverted index answers directly by reading one posting list instead of scanning every document.

reviewQuestions.question: What does the IDF factor accomplish in TF-IDF?
reviewQuestions.answer: IDF down-weights terms that appear in many documents (like 'the') and up-weights rare terms, because rare terms are more discriminative for relevance.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does BM25 normalize by document length?
reviewQuestions.answer: Without length normalization a long document accumulates term matches just by being long. The b parameter scales the score by document length relative to the average so long and short documents compete fairly.

reviewQuestions.question: How is BM25 different from TF-IDF?
reviewQuestions.answer: BM25 adds two things TF-IDF lacks: term-frequency saturation (the k1 parameter, so the 10th occurrence adds little) and document-length normalization (the b parameter). It is TF-IDF with diminishing returns and fairness built in.

reviewQuestions.question: When can BM25 outperform embedding-based retrieval?
reviewQuestions.answer: On exact terms, rare tokens, codes, names, and identifiers — anything where the literal string matters. Embeddings capture meaning but blur exact tokens, so BM25 wins on precision for keyword-literal queries.

reviewQuestions.question: How would you combine BM25 and vector search?
reviewQuestions.answer: Run both retrievers, then fuse their rankings — typically with reciprocal rank fusion, which uses ranks (not incomparable scores). Validate that the fused result beats both single retrievers on an eval set.

reviewQuestions.question: When would you use MRR versus nDCG?
reviewQuestions.answer: MRR rewards getting one correct answer near the top — good for known-item search. nDCG uses graded relevance discounted by rank — good when there are multiple results of varying usefulness.

reviewQuestions.question: Why must the eval query set be frozen before tuning?
reviewQuestions.answer: If you change the eval set while tuning, you are optimizing to a moving target and can no longer tell whether a change is a real improvement or a regression. A frozen set makes comparisons valid.

reviewQuestions.question: Why use reciprocal rank fusion instead of averaging BM25 and cosine scores?
reviewQuestions.answer: BM25 and cosine scores live on different, uncalibrated scales — averaging them is meaningless. RRF uses each result's rank position, which is comparable across retrievers.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is reranking done as a second stage instead of over the whole corpus?
reviewQuestions.answer: Cross-encoder rerankers are accurate but expensive — too slow to run over millions of documents. A cheap retriever narrows to ~100 candidates; the reranker only reorders those, getting precision within a latency budget.

reviewQuestions.question: What does 'distance' mean in an embedding space?
reviewQuestions.answer: An embedding model places semantically similar content close together, so geometric distance approximates semantic dissimilarity. Search becomes finding the nearest vectors to the query vector.

reviewQuestions.question: When do cosine similarity and dot product give the same ranking?
reviewQuestions.answer: When all vectors are L2-normalized to unit length: then dot product equals cosine, so they rank identically. On un-normalized vectors, dot product is also influenced by magnitude.

reviewQuestions.question: How do you return top-k without sorting all n scores?
reviewQuestions.answer: Keep a size-k heap ordered so its root is the current worst survivor — a min-heap when higher score wins, a max-heap when lower distance wins. Push until the heap holds k, then replace the root whenever a candidate beats it. O(n log k) time, O(k) space, and no full sort.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is a brute-force index essential even though it is slow?
reviewQuestions.answer: It is exact — recall is 1.0 by definition. It is the ground-truth oracle against which an approximate index's recall is measured. Without it, ANN recall is unknowable.

reviewQuestions.question: What do the layers in an HNSW graph do?
reviewQuestions.answer: Upper layers are sparse with long-range links for fast coarse navigation; lower layers are dense for fine-grained search. A query takes long hops up top, then descends to refine, so it visits a small fraction of the graph rather than scanning all n. The paper measures polylogarithmic scaling; it is not a proven worst-case bound.

reviewQuestions.question: What does the efSearch parameter trade off in HNSW?
reviewQuestions.answer: efSearch is the size of the dynamic candidate list during search. Larger efSearch explores more of the graph: higher recall but higher latency. It is the main recall/latency knob at query time.

reviewQuestions.question: What happens to recall and latency as you increase nprobe in IVF?
reviewQuestions.answer: nprobe is how many Voronoi cells a query scans. More cells means more vectors examined: higher recall, higher latency. nprobe=1 is fast but misses neighbours near cell boundaries.

reviewQuestions.question: How does product quantization shrink vector memory?
reviewQuestions.answer: It splits each vector into m sub-vectors and replaces each with the 1-byte id of its nearest centroid in a per-sub-space codebook, so the code is m bytes regardless of the original width. A 1536-d float32 vector (6 KB) becomes about 48-192 bytes at typical m, at the cost of approximate distances.

reviewQuestions.question: Compare pre-filtering and post-filtering in vector search.
reviewQuestions.answer: Pre-filtering restricts the candidate set before search — exact, but can be slow inside a graph index. Post-filtering runs ANN then drops non-matches — fast, but may return fewer than k results when matches are sparse.

reviewQuestions.question: Why report a recall/latency curve instead of a single recall number?
reviewQuestions.answer: Recall alone is meaningless without its cost. Every ANN knob trades recall for latency or memory, so the honest artifact is a curve showing the achievable operating points, anchored by brute force at recall 1.0.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is retrieval the quality ceiling of a RAG system?
reviewQuestions.answer: The model can only answer from the context it receives. If retrieval misses the relevant chunk, no amount of model quality recovers the answer — so most 'RAG is bad' problems are retrieval problems.

reviewQuestions.question: When would you choose RAG over fine-tuning?
reviewQuestions.answer: RAG when knowledge changes often, must be cited, or is too large to bake into weights. Fine-tuning when you need to change behavior, format, or style rather than inject facts. They are often combined.

reviewQuestions.question: What is the tradeoff in choosing chunk size?
reviewQuestions.answer: Large chunks dilute embeddings and retrieve irrelevant text alongside the answer; small chunks lose surrounding context and may split an answer. Good chunking respects structure and adds overlap.

reviewQuestions.question: What is the 'lost in the middle' effect and how do you mitigate it?
reviewQuestions.answer: LLMs attend more strongly to the start and end of the context window than the middle. Mitigate by placing the strongest evidence at the edges, deduping, and cutting low-value context rather than overflowing the window.

reviewQuestions.question: Why constrain LLM output to a schema instead of parsing prose?
reviewQuestions.answer: Prose is unreliable to parse and breaks silently. Schema-constrained generation yields a typed object your code can validate and trust — or explicitly reject — making the LLM-to-code boundary safe.

reviewQuestions.question: In tool calling, what does the LLM actually do — and not do?
reviewQuestions.answer: The LLM decides which tool to call and with what arguments (it is the planner). It does not execute anything — your code runs the tool and feeds the result back into context.

reviewQuestions.question: What guardrails keep an agent loop from running away?
reviewQuestions.answer: A hard step/iteration limit, a bounded context (summarize or drop old turns), explicit stopping conditions, and a human-approval gate before irreversible actions.

reviewQuestions.question: Why must model routing be backed by evals?
reviewQuestions.answer: Routing sends some requests to a weaker model to save cost. Without evals you cannot tell whether that routed traffic still meets quality — cost savings would silently come at the price of regressions.

reviewQuestions.question: Why must an LLM-as-judge be validated against human labels?
reviewQuestions.answer: An LLM judge has its own biases and blind spots. If it disagrees with humans, your eval scores are wrong. Validate it on a labelled sample before trusting it to gate releases.

reviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between HTTP 401 and 403?
reviewQuestions.answer: 401 Unauthorized means the request is not authenticated — you have not proven who you are. 403 Forbidden means you are authenticated but not allowed to perform this action.

reviewQuestions.question: How should API keys be stored, and why?
reviewQuestions.answer: Store only a hash of the key, like a password — so a database leak does not expose usable keys. Show the secret once at creation, add a searchable prefix, and support rotation and revocation.

reviewQuestions.question: How does a token bucket differ from a fixed-window counter?
reviewQuestions.answer: A fixed window resets counts on a boundary, allowing up to 2x the limit across the boundary. A token bucket refills continuously, smoothing the rate while still permitting bursts up to the bucket size.

reviewQuestions.question: Why are idempotency keys needed for POST endpoints?
reviewQuestions.answer: Network failures make clients retry, and retrying a non-idempotent POST (like a payment) repeats the effect. An idempotency key lets the server recognize a duplicate and replay the original result instead of re-executing.

reviewQuestions.question: What problem does a dead-letter queue solve?
reviewQuestions.answer: A message that always fails (a poison message) would be retried forever, blocking the queue. A DLQ moves it aside after N attempts so the pipeline keeps flowing and the failure can be inspected.

reviewQuestions.question: Why add jitter to retry backoff?
reviewQuestions.answer: Without jitter, many clients that failed at the same moment retry at the same moment, creating a synchronized thundering herd. Randomized delay spreads the retries out.

reviewQuestions.question: What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
reviewQuestions.answer: When a hot key expires, many concurrent requests all miss and hit the origin at once. Prevent it with a lock/single-flight so only one request recomputes, or with early/probabilistic refresh before expiry.

reviewQuestions.question: What question does each of metrics, traces, and logs answer?
reviewQuestions.answer: Metrics tell you that something is wrong; traces tell you where in the system; logs tell you why. A correlation id stitches them into one story for a request.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is 'exactly-once' delivery usually a myth, and what do you do instead?
reviewQuestions.answer: Failures and retries make true exactly-once delivery effectively impossible end-to-end. Design for at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers, which yields exactly-once *effects*.

reviewQuestions.question: Why should every list endpoint be paginated from day one?
reviewQuestions.answer: An unpaginated list grows without bound and eventually returns huge responses or times out. Adding pagination later is a breaking change, so it should be designed in from the start (cursor-based preferred).

reviewQuestions.question: What is the core tradeoff between JWTs and server sessions?
reviewQuestions.answer: JWTs are stateless and fast to verify but hard to revoke before expiry. Sessions are revocable instantly but require a lookup store. Choose based on how quickly you must be able to revoke access.

reviewQuestions.question: When would you choose an LSM tree over a B-tree?
reviewQuestions.answer: Choose an LSM tree for write-heavy workloads: it turns random writes into sequential ones. Choose a B-tree for read-heavy workloads with in-place updates and predictable read latency.

reviewQuestions.question: Why are B-tree nodes sized to disk pages?
reviewQuestions.answer: Disk and memory move data in pages. Sizing a node to a page means one IO loads many keys, keeping the tree shallow (~3-4 levels) so a lookup costs only a few IOs even for billions of rows.

reviewQuestions.question: Why can reads be slow in an LSM tree, and what helps?
reviewQuestions.answer: A key may live in the memtable or any SSTable, so a read might check several files (read amplification). Bloom filters let a read skip files that definitely lack the key; compaction reduces the file count.

reviewQuestions.question: Why write to a WAL before updating the main data structure?
reviewQuestions.answer: The main structure may be mid-update when a crash hits, leaving it corrupt. An append-only WAL records the intended change durably first, so recovery can replay it and restore a consistent state.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is fsync required for WAL durability?
reviewQuestions.answer: A write() syscall only hands data to the OS page cache, which can be lost on a crash. fsync forces it to stable storage. The write may only be acknowledged to the client after the WAL entry is fsync'd.

reviewQuestions.question: What does compaction cost, and what does it buy?
reviewQuestions.answer: Compaction rewrites data (write amplification, IO spikes) but it reclaims space from tombstones/overwrites and bounds read amplification by reducing the number of files a read must check.

reviewQuestions.question: Why can't you treat object storage like a local disk?
reviewQuestions.answer: Object storage has ~tens-of-ms latency, per-request billing, and no in-place edits. Systems built on it batch data into large immutable segment files and keep a hot cache in front to hide the latency.

reviewQuestions.question: Why split a search platform into an indexing path and a query path?
reviewQuestions.answer: They have opposite requirements: indexing is durable, batchy, and write-optimized; querying is low-latency, cacheable, and read-optimized. Separating them lets each be designed and scaled independently.

reviewQuestions.question: What are the two pipelines in a RAG system, and what binds them?
reviewQuestions.answer: An offline ingestion pipeline (chunk → embed → index) and an online query pipeline (retrieve → rerank → pack → generate). An eval harness binds them — it gates every change to either pipeline.

reviewQuestions.question: What does the dot product measure geometrically?
reviewQuestions.answer: The dot product measures how much one vector projects onto another — alignment. u·v = ||u|| ||v|| cos θ. Zero dot product means orthogonal (perpendicular) vectors.

reviewQuestions.question: How do the columns of a matrix relate to a linear transformation?
reviewQuestions.answer: Each column is where a basis vector lands after the transformation. Matrix multiplication composes transformations: the columns of AB are A applied to the columns of B.

reviewQuestions.question: What is an eigenvector, and why does SVD matter?
reviewQuestions.answer: An eigenvector is a direction unchanged by a matrix except for scaling by the eigenvalue. SVD factors any matrix into rotations and scalings, enabling low-rank approximation (PCA, compression).

reviewQuestions.question: State Bayes' rule and when you need it.
reviewQuestions.answer: P(A|B) = P(B|A)·P(A) / P(B). Use it when you have a likelihood and a prior but need the posterior — e.g. updating disease probability after a test result.

reviewQuestions.question: How does the sample mean relate to expectation?
reviewQuestions.answer: Expectation is the theoretical long-run average of a random variable. The sample mean estimates it from data; by the law of large numbers, the sample mean converges to the expectation as n grows.

reviewQuestions.question: When should you report median instead of mean?
reviewQuestions.answer: When the distribution is skewed or has heavy tails (latency, income, error rates). The median resists outliers; the mean gets pulled by them and misrepresents the typical value.

reviewQuestions.question: What does a 95% confidence interval mean?
reviewQuestions.answer: If you repeated the experiment many times, 95% of the intervals you'd construct would contain the true parameter. It is not 'there is a 95% chance this specific interval contains the truth'.

reviewQuestions.question: What is a p-value, and what is it not?
reviewQuestions.answer: A p-value is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the null is true, nor proof that an effect is large or important.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is least-squares regression called a projection?
reviewQuestions.answer: The fitted values ŷ are the orthogonal projection of the target vector y onto the column space of the feature matrix X. Residuals are perpendicular to that subspace.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does gradient descent step opposite the gradient?
reviewQuestions.answer: The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase. To minimize a loss, move in the opposite direction — the steepest decrease — scaled by a learning rate.

reviewQuestions.question: Convexity makes optimisation easier — but what exactly does it guarantee, and what does it not?
reviewQuestions.answer: It guarantees only that no local minimum is a non-global one, so a descent method cannot get trapped in a worse basin. It does not promise a unique minimiser (a flat valley has many), nor that a minimum exists at all (e^-x descends forever), nor convergence at any step size — too large a step still diverges. Neural losses are non-convex, so none of that holds and we rely on SGD heuristics plus conditioning tricks instead of a guarantee.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is cross-entropy a natural classification loss?
reviewQuestions.answer: Cross-entropy measures the extra surprise (nats/bits) when you use your predicted distribution instead of the true one. Minimizing it pushes predicted probabilities toward the correct class labels.

reviewQuestions.question: How is independence different from mutual exclusivity?
reviewQuestions.answer: Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen (P(A∩B)=0). Independent events can co-occur, and P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). Independence is about information; exclusivity is about overlap.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is f(x) in a PDF not a probability?
reviewQuestions.answer: For continuous random variables, P(X=x)=0. The PDF value f(x) is a density; probability comes from integrating over an interval. Only the integral over a range is between 0 and 1.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does correlation not imply causation?
reviewQuestions.answer: Correlation only measures linear association. A third confounding variable, reverse causality, or coincidence can produce high r without A causing B.

reviewQuestions.question: Define Type I and Type II errors.
reviewQuestions.answer: Type I: reject a true null (false alarm), controlled by α. Type II: fail to reject a false null (missed detection). Power = 1 − P(Type II) for a specific alternative effect size.

reviewQuestions.question: When use Poisson instead of Binomial?
reviewQuestions.answer: Binomial counts successes in n fixed trials with probability p. Poisson models counts of rare events in a fixed interval when n is large and p is small (or events arrive continuously). Poisson is the limit of Binomial under those conditions.

reviewQuestions.question: When is a Normal approximation reasonable for a Binomial?
reviewQuestions.answer: When np and n(1−p) are both moderately large (rule of thumb ≥5–10), the Binomial is well approximated by Normal(np, np(1−p)). Small n or extreme p breaks the approximation.

reviewQuestions.question: What does the Central Limit Theorem say about sample means?
reviewQuestions.answer: For i.i.d. samples with finite variance, the distribution of the sample mean approaches Normal as n grows, regardless of the population shape (with known mean/variance scaling). That justifies z-tests and CIs on means and proportions at scale.

reviewQuestions.question: Standard error vs standard deviation?
reviewQuestions.answer: Standard deviation describes spread of individual observations. Standard error is SD/√n and describes uncertainty in the sample mean (or other estimator). CIs use SE, not raw SD.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is peeking at A/B results mid-test dangerous?
reviewQuestions.answer: Repeated optional stopping inflates false-positive rate far above α. If you check often and stop when p<0.05, you'll find 'significance' by chance even when there is no effect. Pre-register sample size or use sequential testing methods.

reviewQuestions.question: Statistical significance vs statistical power?
reviewQuestions.answer: Significance (α) bounds false alarms when the null is true. Power is the chance to detect a real effect of a given size. Underpowered tests often yield 'not significant' while a meaningful effect exists.

reviewQuestions.question: Credible interval vs confidence interval?
reviewQuestions.answer: A 95% credible interval means the parameter lies in the interval with 95% posterior probability given data and prior. A 95% CI is about the procedure: 95% of such intervals from repeated experiments would contain the true parameter.

reviewQuestions.question: When is Bayesian inference especially useful?
reviewQuestions.answer: With scarce data, hierarchical structure, sequential updating, or when you need a direct distribution over parameters (not just reject/don't reject). Also natural when you have informative priors from past experiments.

reviewQuestions.question: How does MLE relate to cross-entropy loss?
reviewQuestions.answer: Maximizing likelihood for Bernoulli/categorical outcomes is equivalent to minimizing cross-entropy between the true one-hot labels and the model's predicted probabilities. Training classifiers with cross-entropy is MLE under that model.

reviewQuestions.question: Likelihood vs posterior?
reviewQuestions.answer: Likelihood is P(data|θ) as a function of θ with data fixed. Posterior is P(θ|data) ∝ likelihood × prior. MLE picks θ that maximizes likelihood; Bayesian inference integrates the posterior.

reviewQuestions.question: Covariance vs correlation?
reviewQuestions.answer: Covariance measures co-movement in original units (sign matters, scale-dependent). Correlation is covariance divided by both standard deviations, always in [−1,1], unitless and comparable across pairs.

reviewQuestions.question: Explain the bias-variance tradeoff.
reviewQuestions.answer: Simple models have high bias (underfit), low variance. Complex models fit training noise (low bias, high variance). Generalization error is roughly bias² + variance + irreducible noise. Overfitting is excess variance.

reviewQuestions.question: What is matrix rank?
reviewQuestions.answer: Rank is the dimension of the column space — the number of linearly independent columns (equals independent rows). It is the true degrees of freedom of the linear map, not the matrix size.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is PCA a projection?
reviewQuestions.answer: PCA finds an orthogonal basis ordered by variance. Keeping the top k components is the orthogonal projection of centered data onto the k-dimensional subspace that minimizes squared reconstruction error.

reviewQuestions.question: Why model returns instead of prices?
reviewQuestions.answer: Price levels are non-stationary (trend, scale changes). Returns are closer to stable, comparable across assets, and the object of portfolio math. Correlations and regressions on prices are usually misleading.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does stationarity matter for inference?
reviewQuestions.answer: Many statistical tools assume fixed mean/variance and stable dependence structure. Non-stationary series (trending levels, changing vol) make sample moments, correlations, and hypothesis tests unreliable without transformation or regime handling.

reviewQuestions.question: What is the Markov property?
reviewQuestions.answer: Future state depends only on the present state, not the full history: P(X_{t+1}|X_t, X_{t-1},...) = P(X_{t+1}|X_t). Random walks are Markov chains on position.

reviewQuestions.question: What are limitations of the Sharpe ratio?
reviewQuestions.answer: Assumes returns are well-summarized by mean and vol (penalizes upside vol too), sensitive to non-normality and short samples, ignores tail risk and drawdowns, and can be inflated by leverage or in-sample selection.

reviewQuestions.question: Why do most backtests overfit?
reviewQuestions.answer: Researchers try many rules/parameters on the same history (implicit multiple testing), use survivorship-biased universes, omit costs, and lack holdout/walk-forward validation — so in-sample edge is curve-fit, not alpha.

reviewQuestions.question: Synonym expansion improves recall but precision drops. What is the mechanism, and what is the usual mitigation?
reviewQuestions.answer: Every added term matches more documents, including ones where the synonym carries a different sense, and it dilutes the scoring weight of the term the user actually typed. Mitigation is to expand at retrieval only, keep the original terms weighted higher, and let a reranker restore precision.

reviewQuestions.question: Why can recall lost in candidate generation never be recovered by a better ranker?
reviewQuestions.answer: The ranker only reorders what the first stage returned. A document the retrieval step never produced has no score to improve. That is why cheap first-stage recall is tuned separately from precision, and why hybrid retrieval unions lexical and vector candidates before reranking.

reviewQuestions.question: Quality dropped last Tuesday. What must have been logged for you to find the cause?
reviewQuestions.answer: The prompt version and the model version stamped on every request, alongside the rendered input and the output. Prompt text alone is not enough — a provider-side model update changes behaviour with no diff on your side, so both identifiers have to be attached to each logged call.

reviewQuestions.question: A matmul fails with a shape error. What does reading the shapes tell you about what the layer is actually doing?
reviewQuestions.answer: (n, d) @ (d, k) contracts over d and leaves (n, k): n items in, k features out, d is what must agree. The contracted dimension is the one being summed over, so a shape error names exactly which two things you assumed lived in the same space and do not.

reviewQuestions.question: Loss goes down for a while, then spikes to NaN. What does that pattern point at first?
reviewQuestions.answer: A step too large for the local curvature: the update overshoots, the next gradient is larger, and it diverges within a few steps. Lower the learning rate, add warmup, or clip gradient norm. Exploding activations from a bad init or a missing normalisation give the same signature.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does the backward pass need values cached from the forward pass, and what does that cost?
reviewQuestions.answer: Local derivatives depend on the inputs — d(xW)/dW needs x, and d(relu)/dx needs the sign of x. So activations are held in memory until their gradient is consumed. That is why activation memory scales with depth times batch size, and why gradient checkpointing recomputes instead of storing.

reviewQuestions.question: Why are softmax and cross-entropy implemented as one fused op rather than two?
reviewQuestions.answer: Composed, the gradient collapses to (p - y) — one subtraction. Kept separate you compute exp then a log of it, which overflows for large logits and loses precision for small ones. Fusing also enables the log-sum-exp trick of subtracting the max logit.

reviewQuestions.question: What does the W in AdamW change, and why did plain Adam plus L2 not do the same thing?
reviewQuestions.answer: L2 adds the penalty to the gradient, so Adam's per-parameter scaling divides it by the same running second moment — parameters with large gradients get decayed less. AdamW subtracts the decay from the weights directly after the step, making it uniform and decoupled from the adaptive scale.

reviewQuestions.question: Why can you not swap a model's tokenizer for a better one without retraining?
reviewQuestions.answer: Token ids are the model's input vocabulary — each row of the embedding matrix was learned for one specific id. A different tokenizer maps text to different ids, so every embedding lookup returns a vector trained for another token. The tokenizer and the embedding table are one artifact.

reviewQuestions.question: What does perplexity actually measure, and why can two models' perplexities be incomparable?
reviewQuestions.answer: It is the exponential of the mean negative log-likelihood per token — roughly, how many equally likely options the model was choosing between. It is per token, so a different tokenizer changes the token count and the number, even on identical text. Compare only within the same tokenizer and eval set.

reviewQuestions.question: Top-k and top-p both truncate the distribution. When does the difference matter?
reviewQuestions.answer: Top-k always keeps k candidates, so on a confident step it admits k-1 junk tokens, and on a genuinely ambiguous one it cuts good options. Top-p keeps the smallest set summing to p, so the candidate count adapts to how peaked the distribution is.

reviewQuestions.question: Self-attention is permutation-equivariant — shuffle the tokens and the output shuffles with them. What does that force the embedding layer to do, and why?
reviewQuestions.answer: Attention is a weighted sum over a set, so nothing in it distinguishes "the cat sat" from "sat cat the" — the outputs simply permute along with the inputs. Order has to enter through the embedding, as a learned or sinusoidal positional signal added to (or rotated into) the token vector, before attention ever runs. Drop it and the model is a bag of words.

reviewQuestions.question: Why divide the query-key dot product by sqrt(d_k)?
reviewQuestions.answer: With unit-variance q and k, the dot product over d_k dimensions has variance d_k, so scores grow with head width. Large scores drive softmax to one-hot, where its gradient is near zero. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) restores unit variance and keeps the softmax in a trainable range.

reviewQuestions.question: Multi-head attention splits d_model into h heads rather than running h full-width attentions. What does that buy?
reviewQuestions.answer: Cost parity. Each head works in d_model/h dimensions, so h heads together cost about the same FLOPs and parameters as one full-width head, while giving h independent attention patterns. The output projection then mixes the concatenated heads back into d_model.

reviewQuestions.question: Pre-LayerNorm versus post-LayerNorm — why did deep stacks move to pre-norm?
reviewQuestions.answer: Pre-norm keeps a clean, unnormalised residual path from input to output, so gradients reach early layers directly and deep stacks train without a warmup schedule. Post-norm normalises after the residual add, attenuating that path and making very deep models unstable to start.

reviewQuestions.question: What is the single fastest sanity check that your training loop is wired correctly?
reviewQuestions.answer: Overfit one tiny batch. A correct model plus loss plus optimizer can drive loss on 8 examples to near zero in a few hundred steps. If it cannot, the bug is in the code — detached graph, wrong loss reduction, shuffled labels — not in the data or the hyperparameters.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is saving only the weights not enough to resume training?
reviewQuestions.answer: The optimizer carries state — Adam's first and second moment estimates, the LR-schedule step count, the gradient scaler, and the data-loader position. Restarting without it resets the moments to zero, so the first steps after resume are effectively unwarmed and the loss spikes.

reviewQuestions.question: What do rank r and alpha each control in LoRA, and what does r actually limit?
reviewQuestions.answer: The update is B@A with inner dimension r, scaled by alpha/r. r caps the rank of the weight change — how many independent directions the adapter can move — so too small a rank underfits genuinely new capability. alpha only rescales, letting you change r without re-tuning the learning rate.

reviewQuestions.question: In GRPO-style RL alignment, why are advantages computed relative to a group of completions for the same prompt, and why is importance sampling needed?
reviewQuestions.answer: The LM is a policy: sample several completions per prompt, score them, and push token probabilities toward better ones. Group-relative advantages (reward minus group mean, scaled by std) tell the model which completion beat its siblings on the same query. Importance sampling corrects for reusing rollouts from an older policy when training off-policy, and clipping keeps updates stable.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does near-duplicate removal matter more than exact deduplication for a training corpus?
reviewQuestions.answer: Exact matches are rare after crawling; boilerplate, mirrors, and templated pages differ by a few characters yet teach the same tokens repeatedly. Left in, they inflate memorisation and can leak into eval sets. Near-dup detection (MinHash/SimHash over shingles) is what actually finds them.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does the main thread have to be kept out of browser inference, and what does that force into the design?
reviewQuestions.answer: A forward pass blocks the event loop, so the page freezes mid-generation. The model runs in a Web Worker, which means weights and tensors cross a postMessage boundary — hence transferable ArrayBuffers, OPFS for caching the weights between sessions, and a streaming token protocol back to the UI.

reviewQuestions.question: Your WebGPU matmul is far slower than expected. What are the two usual causes, and neither is the arithmetic?
reviewQuestions.answer: Transfer and compilation. Every CPU-GPU copy and every mapAsync readback stalls the pipeline, so per-op round trips destroy the win — keep tensors resident on device. And shader compilation happens at pipeline creation, so the first dispatch pays a cost that must be warmed up, not measured.

reviewQuestions.question: Held-out loss improved but the A/B test was flat. Name two explanations that are not "the metric is wrong".
reviewQuestions.answer: The offline set no longer matches live traffic, so you improved on a distribution users do not send. Or the gain is real but not on the axis the product is bottlenecked by — better on average while the failure cases that drive abandonment are unchanged. Test-set leakage is the third suspect.

reviewQuestions.question: Why must a webhook receiver return 200 before doing the work, and what does that force on you?
reviewQuestions.answer: Providers time out fast and retry on non-2xx, so slow processing produces duplicate deliveries and, eventually, disabled endpoints. Acknowledge then enqueue. That makes the handler asynchronous, so the receiver must be idempotent on the event id and must surface failures itself — the provider will not.

reviewQuestions.question: A job worker dies mid-task. Why does at-least-once delivery follow, and what does that force on the job?
reviewQuestions.answer: The queue cannot tell a crashed worker from a slow one, so it redelivers when the visibility timeout expires. That means every job must be idempotent — keyed on a natural id so a repeat is a no-op — because exactly-once delivery does not exist, only exactly-once effect.

reviewQuestions.question: The charge succeeded at the processor but your service crashed before writing the row. What mechanism recovers this, and why is a retry not enough?
reviewQuestions.answer: Daily reconciliation against the processor's ledger — you cannot know from your own data that money moved. A retry with the same idempotency key is what stops a second charge, but only reconciliation finds the state you never recorded. Money truth lives at the processor; your database is a replica.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does a column store compress so much better than a row store on the same data?
reviewQuestions.answer: A column holds values of one type from one domain, so runs repeat: run-length, dictionary, and delta encoding all become effective. A row interleaves an int, a timestamp, and a string, so there is little local redundancy to exploit. Better compression also means fewer bytes read per scan.

reviewQuestions.question: What is a covering index, and how does it change the cost of a query?
reviewQuestions.answer: An index that already contains every column the query needs, so the engine answers from the index alone and skips the lookup back into the base table. That removes one random read per matching row — often the dominant cost. The price is a wider index and more write amplification.

reviewQuestions.question: B-tree versus LSM: which one has read amplification and which has write amplification, and where does each come from?
reviewQuestions.answer: B-trees write-amplify: a one-row update rewrites a whole page, plus the WAL. LSM trees read-amplify: a key may live in the memtable or any level, so a lookup probes several files (bloom filters cut this). LSM then pays its own write amplification later, during compaction.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is changing the shard key later so much harder than choosing a different index?
reviewQuestions.answer: The shard key decides physical placement, so changing it means moving essentially every row across nodes while serving traffic, usually via dual-writes and a backfill with a cutover. An index is local to a node and can be built in the background.

reviewQuestions.question: A user updates their profile and the next page shows the old value. Name the guarantee that is missing and two ways to provide it.
reviewQuestions.answer: Read-your-writes (read-after-write) consistency. Provide it by routing that user's reads to the leader for a short window after their write, or by having the client carry the log position of its write and requiring the replica to have caught up to it before serving.

reviewQuestions.question: What does PACELC add that CAP leaves out, and why does it describe real systems better?
reviewQuestions.answer: The else branch: when there is no partition, you still trade Latency against Consistency. Partitions are rare, so CAP describes a small fraction of a system's life. Every synchronous-quorum write pays latency for consistency on a perfectly healthy day — that is the choice you actually live with.

reviewQuestions.question: When does "is-a" inheritance actively hurt, and what is the tell?
reviewQuestions.answer: When behaviour varies along more than one axis — inheritance fixes the variation at compile time and you end up with one class per combination. The tell: a subclass overrides a method to do nothing. That means the is-a claim is false and you wanted composition.

reviewQuestions.question: Your code is full of `if (paid && !refunded && shippedAt == null)`. What does converting to a state machine actually buy you?
reviewQuestions.answer: The legal transitions move into one table, so an illegal move is rejected in one place instead of every caller remembering the right conjunction. Adding a state becomes one row plus its edges, not a grep across the codebase.

reviewQuestions.question: Strategy pattern versus a switch statement — what concretely changes?
reviewQuestions.answer: A switch keeps every variant in the caller, so adding one edits shared code and the caller depends on all of them. Strategy puts each behind an interface, so a variant is a new file and the choice can come from config, tenant, or experiment at runtime. You pay in indirection.

reviewQuestions.question: What debugging capability do you lose when direct calls become pub/sub, and how do you get it back?
reviewQuestions.answer: The call stack stops explaining why something ran — the publisher does not know its subscribers. You recover it with a correlation id carried on every event, an ordered event log, and tracing spans linking each publish to each handler.

reviewQuestions.question: What is the concrete signal that a factory earns its keep rather than just adding a layer?
reviewQuestions.answer: Adding the fourth variant requires no change at any call site. If every new type still forces callers to edit, the factory only relocated the switch. Singleton is the odd one out — it mostly hides global state and makes tests order-dependent.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does decoration beat subclassing when features combine, and what does it cost?
reviewQuestions.answer: Subclassing needs a class per combination — n features means up to 2^n classes. Decorators wrap at runtime so n small classes compose freely. The costs: order becomes semantic (retry-around-cache differs from cache-around-retry) and stack traces get deep.

reviewQuestions.question: Two threads deadlock. What is the discipline that prevents it, and why is adding a lock usually the wrong fix?
reviewQuestions.answer: A global lock ordering: every path acquires locks in the same sequence, so no cycle can form. Adding locks adds edges to that graph and more chances for a cycle. The cheaper fixes are usually structural — one writer, or one database transaction doing the whole update.

reviewQuestions.question: What must a command object carry to support undo, and where does undo stop working?
reviewQuestions.answer: Enough to invert itself: the inverse operation plus whatever state it overwrote, or a snapshot. It stops working once the effect has left the system — email sent, payment captured, webhook delivered. Those need a compensating action, not an undo.

reviewQuestions.question: When should a booking flow take a pessimistic lock instead of an optimistic version check?
reviewQuestions.answer: When collisions are frequent and a retry is expensive or user-visible — one seat, many simultaneous bidders. Optimistic wins when conflicts are rare because it costs nothing on the happy path. Decide from the measured collision rate, not intuition.

reviewQuestions.question: Client-side prediction hides latency. What does the client have to keep in order to correct itself?
reviewQuestions.answer: A buffer of unacknowledged inputs with sequence numbers. When the server's authoritative state arrives it is behind, so the client rewinds to it and replays every input newer than the acknowledged one. Without that buffer, reconciliation snaps the player backwards visibly.

reviewQuestions.question: Round-robin is distributing requests evenly but tail latency is bad. What is the likely cause and the fix?
reviewQuestions.answer: Requests are not equal cost, so one server queues behind a slow request while others idle. Least-outstanding-requests routes on observed load rather than turn order; power-of-two-choices gets most of that benefit without any global state.

reviewQuestions.question: The ring already limits key movement to about 1/N. So why are virtual nodes needed?
reviewQuestions.answer: One point per server divides the ring unevenly by chance, so some servers own far larger arcs. Many positions per server averages the arcs out, and it spreads a departing server's keys across all survivors instead of dumping them on its single successor.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does a majority quorum give consensus its safety property?
reviewQuestions.answer: Any two majorities of the same cluster must share at least one node, so a newly elected leader's quorum necessarily contains a node that saw the previous leader's committed entries. That overlap is what makes committed data impossible to lose — and why an even-sized cluster buys no extra fault tolerance.

reviewQuestions.question: A remote call times out. What do you actually know about whether it executed?
reviewQuestions.answer: Nothing. The request may never have arrived, may have executed and had its reply lost, or may still be running. That ambiguity is why retries need idempotency keys, why fencing tokens exist, and why a timeout must be paired with a way to discover the real outcome later.

reviewQuestions.question: Why do WebSockets constrain your load balancer in ways HTTP requests do not?
reviewQuestions.answer: The connection is long-lived and pinned to one server, so the balancer cannot rebalance mid-connection and a deploy drops every socket it holds. Server-side state means fan-out needs a cross-node bus (Redis pub/sub, a broker) because the recipient is rarely on the node that received the message.

reviewQuestions.question: Describe the hybrid feed strategy and say exactly where the merge happens.
reviewQuestions.answer: Fan out on write for ordinary accounts; skip fan-out above a follower threshold. At read time the precomputed timeline is merged with a live pull of the few high-fanout accounts the user follows — a small k-way merge by timestamp, done per request.

reviewQuestions.question: What does adaptive bitrate demand of the encoding pipeline?
reviewQuestions.answer: The same content encoded at several bitrates and cut into short segments (2-10s) whose boundaries align across every rendition, on keyframes. That alignment is what lets the player switch quality between segments without a stall or a visible seek.

reviewQuestions.question: Why can a geohash prefix search miss the true nearest neighbour?
reviewQuestions.answer: Geohash is a space-filling curve, so two points metres apart can sit either side of a cell boundary and share no prefix. Correct nearest-neighbour search must also scan the eight adjacent cells, or use S2 / a quadtree that handles boundaries explicitly.

reviewQuestions.question: What must be true of the server for OT to be correct, and why do CRDTs not need it?
reviewQuestions.answer: OT needs a central authority to order concurrent operations and transform each against those already applied; correctness rests on transformation functions that are famously hard to get right. A CRDT puts merge into the data type, so any delivery order converges — paid for with metadata that grows with edit history.

reviewQuestions.question: You need to know whether any two numbers in an array sum to a target. What do you key the hash map on, and what does that buy you?
reviewQuestions.answer: Key on values already seen. For each x, look up target - x; if it is there you have the pair. The map answers "have I seen the complement?" in O(1), collapsing the nested loop into one pass — paid for with O(n) memory.

reviewQuestions.question: On a sorted array, why can a two-pointer scan discard many candidate pairs at once instead of one at a time?
reviewQuestions.answer: The comparison is decisive. If a[lo] + a[hi] is too small, a[hi] was the largest possible partner for a[lo], so no pair using a[lo] can ever work and lo advances — eliminating a whole row of pairs. Sortedness is what makes that elimination sound.

reviewQuestions.question: Why must the shrink step be a `while` loop rather than an `if`?
reviewQuestions.answer: One expansion can break the constraint by more than one element, so the left edge may need to move several times before the invariant holds again. An `if` shrinks once, leaves the window invalid, and every answer computed after that reads a broken state.

reviewQuestions.question: In a monotonic stack, what does the stack hold at any moment, and what does a pop mean?
reviewQuestions.answer: It holds items whose answer is still unknown, kept in sorted order by value. Pushing a new element pops everyone it beats — and the new element is precisely their answer (next greater or next smaller). Each index is pushed and popped once, so the scan is O(n).

reviewQuestions.question: What property must hold before you can binary-search the answer space, and how do you check it?
reviewQuestions.answer: The predicate must be monotonic in x — false...false then true...true, or the reverse. Test it by asking whether condition(x) implies condition(x+1). Without monotonicity, halving throws away a region that could still contain the answer.

reviewQuestions.question: What does a fast/slow pointer pair give you that a single pointer cannot?
reviewQuestions.answer: A ratio. Slow moves one node, fast moves two, so when fast reaches the end slow sits at the midpoint. If there is a cycle, fast must eventually lap slow, so they meet. Midpoint and cycle detection in one pass with O(1) extra memory.

reviewQuestions.question: In a recursive tree solution, why separate "the answer" from "the value returned to the parent"?
reviewQuestions.answer: They are often different quantities. In max-path-sum the parent can only extend one branch, so you return the best single-branch value while a global variable records the best split-at-this-node value. Conflating them lets paths fork twice and gives wrong answers.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does trie prefix lookup cost the same whether you stored a thousand words or a million?
reviewQuestions.answer: Lookup walks one node per prefix character, so the cost is O(len(prefix)); branching happens inside a node, not across the dataset. The price is memory — roughly one node per distinct prefix, which is why a sorted array plus binary search is often smaller.

reviewQuestions.question: A size-k heap is O(n log k) and sorting is O(n log n). When is sorting still the better choice?
reviewQuestions.answer: When k approaches n (the log terms converge and the heap adds overhead), when you need the full ordering anyway, or when n is small enough that constant factors and code simplicity dominate. The heap wins when k is tiny relative to n.

reviewQuestions.question: What exactly has to be undone after a recursive call returns, and what breaks if you forget?
reviewQuestions.answer: Every mutation made before recursing: the partial candidate, visited marks, and any running aggregate. Forgetting leaks state into sibling branches, so later branches explore from a corrupted prefix and emit duplicates or silently skip valid answers.

reviewQuestions.question: In BFS, do you mark a node visited when you enqueue it or when you dequeue it — and why does it matter?
reviewQuestions.answer: On enqueue. Marking on dequeue lets the same node be pushed once per incoming edge before it is ever processed, so the queue grows to O(E) duplicates and the same node is expanded repeatedly. Correctness survives, performance does not.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does Dijkstra give wrong answers on negative edges when Bellman-Ford does not?
reviewQuestions.answer: Dijkstra finalizes a node the moment it is popped, betting that no later path can be shorter — a negative edge can make one shorter afterwards. Bellman-Ford never finalizes: it relaxes every edge V-1 times, so a late improvement still propagates through the graph.

reviewQuestions.question: What do path compression and union by rank each contribute, and why is one alone not enough?
reviewQuestions.answer: Union by rank keeps trees shallow by hanging the smaller tree under the larger; path compression flattens the whole path to the root on every find. Either optimization alone gives O(log n) amortized; together they give inverse-Ackermann, effectively constant.

reviewQuestions.question: The recurrence looks right but the answers are wrong. What is the first thing to check about iteration order?
reviewQuestions.answer: That every state the recurrence reads is already computed. dp[i] depending on dp[i-1] needs ascending order; dp[i] depending on dp[i+1] needs descending. The rolled 1D knapsack iterates capacity backwards for exactly this reason — forwards lets one item be used twice.

reviewQuestions.question: In edit distance, state precisely what dp[i][j] means and what the three predecessor cells correspond to.
reviewQuestions.answer: dp[i][j] is the minimum number of edits turning the first i characters of A into the first j of B. dp[i-1][j] is a delete, dp[i][j-1] is an insert, dp[i-1][j-1] is a replace (free when the characters match). Naming the state exactly is what makes the transitions fall out.

reviewQuestions.question: What is an exchange argument, and why does a greedy algorithm need one?
reviewQuestions.answer: You show any optimal solution can be rewritten into the greedy one without getting worse — swap the optimum's first differing choice for greedy's and argue it is no worse. Without that proof greedy has no reason to be correct, and it fails silently rather than loudly.

reviewQuestions.question: Merging overlapping intervals sorts by start time; picking the most non-overlapping intervals sorts by end time. Why the difference?
reviewQuestions.answer: Merging processes intervals in the order they open, so any overlap is with the block currently being built. Scheduling wants the resource freed as early as possible, and the interval ending soonest leaves the most room for everything after it — that is the exchange argument.

reviewQuestions.question: What does the sign of the 2D cross product tell you, and which problems does that single test solve?
reviewQuestions.answer: For vectors AB and AC the sign says whether C lies left of, right of, or on line AB (counter-clockwise, clockwise, collinear). That one test drives orientation, segment-intersection, and convex-hull construction — with no trigonometry and no division.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does `n & (n - 1)` clear the lowest set bit, and what two things does that give you?
reviewQuestions.answer: n-1 flips the lowest set bit to 0 and sets every bit below it to 1; the AND keeps the higher bits and zeroes that whole tail. Looping on it counts set bits in as many iterations as there are bits set, and `n & (n-1) == 0` tests for a power of two.

reviewQuestions.question: The room agreed and nothing changed two weeks later. What is the actual evidence that you influenced anyone?
reviewQuestions.answer: Changed defaults, not nods. Someone reprioritised their sprint, wrote the doc, or made your argument in a room you were not in. Agreement in a meeting is free; if no behaviour or artefact moved, you got politeness.

reviewQuestions.question: How do you tell a disagreement about facts from a disagreement about priorities, and why does it matter?
reviewQuestions.answer: Ask each side what evidence would change their mind. If an answer exists it is factual — go get the data. If nobody can name any, it is a priorities conflict and more data will not settle it: escalate to whoever owns the tradeoff or run a reversible experiment.

reviewQuestions.question: What separates a bad decision from a bad outcome, and what do you have to write down to tell them apart later?
reviewQuestions.answer: Outcomes are noisy; the decision is the reasoning available at the time. Record the options considered, the assumption the choice rests on, and the observation that would falsify it. Without that, hindsight rewrites every unlucky bet as a mistake.

reviewQuestions.question: Cross-team friction gets blamed on personalities. What is usually the real cause, and what is the concrete fix?
reviewQuestions.answer: Unclear ownership and unstated expectations — each side assuming the other holds a boundary. The fix is written down: who owns each interface, what response time the other side can rely on, and what happens when it slips. Chemistry rarely survives an undefined boundary.

reviewQuestions.question: What makes a post-mortem blameless in practice rather than just in name?
reviewQuestions.answer: Asking how the system made the mistake look reasonable at the time — what signal was missing, what the tooling permitted. Naming a person ends the investigation early and teaches everyone to hide the next incident. Actions must land on systems and defaults, with an owner and a date.

reviewQuestions.question: What is the concrete test for whether an explanation landed?
reviewQuestions.answer: The listener can make their next decision without a follow-up question, or can restate the tradeoff in their own words. Not whether they nodded. Optimising to sound rigorous instead of passing that test is optimising the wrong thing.

reviewQuestions.question: How can you tell a real prioritisation from an ordered wish list?
reviewQuestions.answer: A real one names what is being dropped and who was told. If everything is still "in progress" and nothing carries an explicit not-now, you sequenced items rather than prioritising, and the cut will happen implicitly through whatever slips.

reviewQuestions.question: "Refuse a tradeoff everyone accepts" is the pitch. How do you tell a real one from wishful thinking?
reviewQuestions.answer: A real one names the constraint that forced the tradeoff and what changed to weaken it — cheaper hardware, a new algorithm, a new distribution channel. With no identified constraint that actually moved, you are declaring the tradeoff away, not beating it.

reviewQuestions.question: A customer asks for a specific feature. What do you establish before building it?
reviewQuestions.answer: The problem behind the request — what were they trying to do when they hit the wall — and whether it generalises beyond this one account. A single complaint is a hypothesis. Building the literal ask usually ships their workaround rather than fixing their problem.

reviewQuestions.question: Where is the line between ownership and heroics?
reviewQuestions.answer: Ownership closes the loop and leaves the system better: the fix, a guardrail so it cannot recur, and a handoff so the next person does not need you. Heroics fix it silently at 2am and leave the same hole. The test is whether anyone else could handle it next time.

reviewQuestions.question: Your positioning statement is completely true. Why might it still be worthless?
reviewQuestions.answer: Because it excludes nobody. A position is defined by the alternative you beat and the buyer you are explicitly not for. If three competitors could swap their logo in and the sentence stays true, you wrote a category description.

reviewQuestions.question: Traffic is high, conversion is low, and the copy is accurate. What do you check first?
reviewQuestions.answer: Message-to-intent match: what the visitor searched or clicked versus what the hero promises. Accurate but generic copy loses to a headline naming the visitor's situation. Second, count the primary calls to action — more than one splits the decision and both lose.

reviewQuestions.question: Every on-page basic is correct and the page still does not rank. What is the usual reason?
reviewQuestions.answer: On-page is a qualifier, not a ranker. Either competing results have more depth and more credible inbound links for that query, or the page misreads intent — informational content served to a transactional search. Neither is fixed by more tags.

reviewQuestions.question: What makes a metric a guardrail rather than an input metric, and why must the tree have one?
reviewQuestions.answer: An input metric is something you are trying to move; a guardrail is something you must not break while moving it. Without one, every north-star gain can be bought with a hidden cost — engagement up while retention or latency quietly degrades.

reviewQuestions.question: What does virtual memory actually buy beyond "more memory than you have"?
reviewQuestions.answer: Isolation and indirection. Each process gets its own address space, so a bad pointer cannot reach another process; and because the mapping is per-page, the kernel can share read-only pages, copy-on-write a fork, map a file, and relocate physical memory without the program knowing.

reviewQuestions.question: A TCP connection is "reliable". Name two failures it does not protect you from.
reviewQuestions.answer: A dead peer — with no data flowing, a host that vanished looks identical to an idle one until a write eventually times out, which is why applications need their own heartbeats. And duplicate application-level effects: TCP delivers bytes once, but your retry after a timeout can still submit the same request twice.

reviewQuestions.question: Two loops do the same arithmetic on the same array and one is many times slower. What is the usual cause?
reviewQuestions.answer: Access pattern versus cache line. A sequential walk brings in 64 bytes and uses all of them, and the prefetcher stays ahead; a strided or pointer-chasing walk uses one value per line and defeats prefetch. The FLOPs are identical — the memory traffic is not.

reviewQuestions.question: Mean latency improved after your change and p99 got worse. What class of cause should you suspect?
reviewQuestions.answer: Something that batches or defers work: a larger buffer, a bigger GC heap, a coarser lock. Average throughput rises because the amortised cost falls, but the occasional flush, collection, or convoy lands entirely on one request. Tail latency is about the variance you introduced, not the mean.

reviewQuestions.question: What does "fail closed" mean at a trust boundary, and why is it a design decision rather than an implementation detail?
reviewQuestions.answer: When the check cannot complete — the auth service is down, the policy will not parse — the request is denied rather than allowed. It is a design decision because failing closed converts a security failure into an availability failure, and that tradeoff must be chosen deliberately per boundary.

reviewQuestions.question: What is a failure domain, and why does multi-AZ buy something multi-instance does not?
reviewQuestions.answer: A failure domain is the blast radius of one correlated failure — a host, a rack, a power zone, a region, a control plane. Three instances in one AZ share the AZ's fate, so they are one domain wearing three hats. Spreading across AZs is what makes the failures independent.

reviewQuestions.question: Kubernetes is described as a reconciliation system. What does that actually change about how it behaves?
reviewQuestions.answer: There is no imperative apply-then-done. A controller repeatedly compares declared state to observed state and takes one corrective step, forever. So it is self-healing and order-independent, but a change can silently never converge, and the honest debugging question is which controller is failing to reconcile.

reviewQuestions.question: Why must promotion move the same artifact rather than rebuild per environment?
reviewQuestions.answer: A rebuild can differ — dependency resolution, base image, build-time config — so the thing you tested in staging is not the thing that reaches production. Build once, tag it, and inject environment differences as configuration at deploy time, so the tested bytes are the shipped bytes.

reviewQuestions.question: What does preemption solve that priority queues alone do not?
reviewQuestions.answer: Priority decides who gets the next free slot; it does nothing when every slot is already held by long-running low-priority work. Preemption reclaims a running slot, which is what bounds the wait for high-priority work — at the cost that evicted jobs must be checkpointable or safely restartable.

reviewQuestions.question: What is an error budget for, and what should happen when it is exhausted?
reviewQuestions.answer: It converts an SLO into a spending limit: 99.9% availability means 0.1% is allowed to be spent on releases and risk. When it runs out the policy is to stop shipping features and spend on reliability. Without that consequence the SLO is a dashboard number, not a control.

reviewQuestions.question: You have metrics and logs. What does a trace add that neither gives you?
reviewQuestions.answer: Causal structure across services for one request. Metrics aggregate away the individual, and logs are per-service lines with no parentage, so neither can tell you which downstream call consumed the latency in this slow request. That requires propagated context and parent-child spans.

reviewQuestions.question: Rank containers, microVMs, and V8 isolates on isolation strength versus startup cost, and say what drives the difference.
reviewQuestions.answer: Isolates start in about a millisecond and share one process, so a runtime escape is total; containers share the host kernel, so the syscall surface is the boundary; microVMs bring their own kernel behind a hypervisor and cost tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Density and isolation trade directly against each other.

reviewQuestions.question: What is drift, and why does a declarative tool need a plan step rather than just applying?
reviewQuestions.answer: Drift is reality diverging from the declared state — a manual console change, an autoscaler, a deleted resource. The plan is the diff against observed state, which is the only place a destructive action (replace, delete) becomes visible before it happens. Applying blind converts drift into an outage.

reviewQuestions.question: Kafka guarantees ordering per partition. What does that force on your partition key choice?
reviewQuestions.answer: Anything that must be processed in order has to share a key so it lands in one partition — usually the entity id. That makes ordering and parallelism directly opposed: a coarse key serialises unrelated work, a fine key lets two events for the same entity be handled out of order.

reviewQuestions.question: Durable execution replays workflow code after a crash. What does that require of the code you write?
reviewQuestions.answer: Determinism. Replay re-executes the function against the recorded history, so the same decisions must be reached — no wall-clock reads, no random, no direct I/O, and no branching on data that could change. Anything non-deterministic goes in an activity, whose result is recorded once and replayed from history.

reviewQuestions.question: What is a fencing token, and which failure does it stop that a lease timeout alone does not?
reviewQuestions.answer: A monotonically increasing number issued with a lock; the storage layer rejects any write carrying a token older than the highest it has seen. It stops the paused-then-resumed holder: a process that stalled past its lease expiry, lost the lock, then woke up and wrote as if it still held it.

reviewQuestions.question: Snapshot isolation prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads but is not serializable. What anomaly survives, and what fixes it?
reviewQuestions.answer: Write skew: two transactions read an overlapping set, each checks an invariant that still holds, and each writes a disjoint row — together breaking the invariant (both doctors go off call). Fixes are SELECT FOR UPDATE on the read set, a materialized conflict row, or serializable snapshot isolation.

reviewQuestions.question: The plan looks reasonable but the query is slow. What estimate is usually wrong, and why does it compound?
reviewQuestions.answer: Cardinality — the row count coming out of a join or filter. Correlated predicates break the independence assumption and errors multiply along the join tree, so an off-by-10 at the bottom becomes off-by-1000 at the top, and the optimizer picks a nested loop where it needed a hash join.

reviewQuestions.question: What does an open table format (Iceberg, Delta) add on top of Parquet files in object storage?
reviewQuestions.answer: A metadata layer listing which files make up the table at each snapshot. That gives atomic commits, time travel, and schema evolution over a store with no rename or multi-object transaction — and it lets the engine prune files by statistics instead of listing a prefix.

reviewQuestions.question: You have a fixed compute budget. What do scaling laws tell you about splitting it between model size and tokens?
reviewQuestions.answer: There is an optimum: for a given FLOP budget, parameters and training tokens should grow together rather than pouring everything into size. Chinchilla showed the previous generation was badly undertrained. If the model will be served heavily, deliberately overshoot on tokens — inference cost tracks parameters, not tokens.

reviewQuestions.question: You quantized to int4 and memory dropped but throughput did not. What went wrong?
reviewQuestions.answer: The format has no matching kernel, so weights are dequantized back to fp16 before every matmul. The memory win is real; the compute win only arrives when the hardware has native support for the format and the layout matches what the kernel expects.

reviewQuestions.question: "Open weights" is not "open source". Name what you still do not get, and the one packaging detail that breaks deployments quietly.
reviewQuestions.answer: You get inspectable parameters, not the training data, the training code, or unrestricted rights — many licenses cap commercial use or restrict fields. The quiet breaker is the chat template: apply the wrong prompt format and quality collapses in a way that looks like a bad model rather than a config error.

reviewQuestions.question: Prefill and decode have very different hardware profiles. Name each and say why it drives the scheduler's design.
reviewQuestions.answer: Prefill processes the whole prompt at once and is compute-bound; decode emits one token per step per sequence and is memory-bandwidth-bound. Batching only helps decode, so the scheduler must interleave the two — chunking long prefills so they do not stall every decoding request behind them.

reviewQuestions.question: What does continuous batching change relative to static batching, and where does the throughput actually come from?
reviewQuestions.answer: Static batching holds every slot until the slowest sequence finishes, so short requests idle the GPU waiting. Continuous batching re-forms the batch each decoding step and admits a queued request into the freed slot immediately. The gain is eliminated bubble time, not faster kernels.

reviewQuestions.question: What fragmentation problem does PagedAttention solve, and what capability falls out of it for free?
reviewQuestions.answer: Contiguous per-request KV allocation must reserve for the maximum possible length, so most of the reservation is never used and cannot be lent out. Paging into fixed blocks with a block table removes that waste — and because blocks are shared by reference, identical prompt prefixes cost one copy.

reviewQuestions.question: FlashAttention computes exact attention yet is much faster. Where does the speed come from if the arithmetic is unchanged?
reviewQuestions.answer: From not writing the N-by-N attention matrix to HBM. It tiles Q, K, V into SRAM and fuses matmul, softmax, and the value multiply into one pass, using online (streaming) softmax so no tile needs the global max in advance. Attention is bandwidth-bound, so removing the traffic is the win.

reviewQuestions.question: Speculative decoding runs two models yet is faster, and the output distribution is unchanged. Explain both claims.
reviewQuestions.answer: The target model verifies k drafted tokens in a single forward pass, and decode is bandwidth-bound, so verifying k costs roughly what one token cost. Correctness comes from the rejection-sampling step: accept each draft token with probability p_target/p_draft and resample from the corrected residual otherwise.

reviewQuestions.question: nvidia-smi reports 100% utilization but throughput is poor. Why is that number misleading, and what do you measure instead?
reviewQuestions.answer: It reports the fraction of time at least one kernel was resident — not whether the SMs or the memory bus were doing useful work. Measure achieved occupancy, memory-bandwidth utilisation, and the arithmetic intensity of the hot kernels to tell compute-bound from memory-bound from launch-bound.

reviewQuestions.question: Why do TTFT and inter-token latency pull the scheduler in opposite directions?
reviewQuestions.answer: Time to first token needs prompts admitted and prefilled promptly; inter-token latency needs the decode batch left undisturbed, because every admitted prefill steals a step from every sequence already generating. Larger batches raise throughput and worsen both. You pick a point on the frontier, not all three.

reviewQuestions.question: A model fits in device RAM and still runs badly on a phone. What is the constraint you overlooked?
reviewQuestions.answer: Sustained power and thermals. Mobile silicon boosts briefly then throttles, so the benchmark you measured cold is not the steady state. Memory bandwidth is the other one — decode is bandwidth-bound, and a phone has a fraction of a GPU's, so quantization buys speed as much as it buys space.

reviewQuestions.question: For single-stream LLM decoding, which hardware number predicts speed best, and why is it not peak TFLOPs?
reviewQuestions.answer: Memory bandwidth. Each token reads the whole weight set once, doing about two FLOPs per byte fetched, so the matrix engines are starved and the roofline lands in the bandwidth-bound region. Peak TFLOPs starts to matter only when batching pushes arithmetic intensity up.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is summarising old turns into the prompt not the same as giving an agent memory?
reviewQuestions.answer: A summary is lossy and irreversible: once compacted you cannot recover the detail a later step needs, and errors in the summary become facts. Real memory keeps the raw event history addressable, stores durable facts retrievably with provenance and expiry, and treats the prompt as a working set fetched from those.

reviewQuestions.question: MCP standardises how a host discovers and calls tools. Name what it deliberately does not give you.
reviewQuestions.answer: Trust. The protocol carries capability descriptions and results; it does not authenticate the user to the downstream system, authorize the specific action, validate arguments, or decide what needs human approval. A tool description is attacker-controlled text, so a connected server is untrusted input, not a trusted extension.

reviewQuestions.question: When does splitting work across agents make results worse rather than better?
reviewQuestions.answer: When subtasks share state or the result cannot be verified independently. Each handoff re-serialises context through natural language, losing detail and adding a chance to misinterpret, and errors compound with no arbiter. Multiple agents pay off only for cleanly separable work with a checkable output.

reviewQuestions.question: An agent crashes after calling a payment API but before recording the result. What makes recovery safe?
reviewQuestions.answer: A side-effect identity assigned before the call — an idempotency key persisted with the intent — so on resume the same key either replays the recorded outcome or is rejected as a duplicate by the provider. Recording after the fact cannot work: the crash window is exactly where the ambiguity lives.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is an agent treated as an untrusted principal even when the user is trusted?
reviewQuestions.answer: Because its instructions come partly from data it reads — a web page, an issue, a tool description — so any content it touches can attempt to steer it. The user's trust does not transfer to the text. Hence scoped short-lived capabilities, no ambient secrets, and approval gates on irreversible effects.

reviewQuestions.question: Screenshot-plus-coordinates versus the accessibility tree: what does each get right and wrong?
reviewQuestions.answer: Pixels work on anything, including canvas and native apps, but grounding is brittle to layout shifts, scroll position, and resolution. The accessibility tree gives stable named elements and is cheap to read, but is missing or wrong on custom widgets. Robust agents use the tree first and fall back to vision.

reviewQuestions.question: Why do agent-to-agent messages need typed status and provenance rather than prose?
reviewQuestions.answer: A receiver cannot branch on prose: "mostly done" has no failure path, and there is no way to tell an observation from an inference. Typed identity, intent, status, result, and error make retries, timeouts, and escalation mechanical — and provenance lets a reviewer check the claim against its source.

reviewQuestions.question: What does a lease give a scheduled agent that a cron entry alone does not?
reviewQuestions.answer: Mutual exclusion under failure. Cron fires on every instance and again on the next tick, so a slow or crashed run overlaps itself. A lease with a heartbeat lets exactly one worker hold the job, makes a dead holder's expiry detectable, and gives cancellation and deadlines something to act on.

reviewQuestions.question: A model scores well on a public coding benchmark. Name the two threats to that score's validity.
reviewQuestions.answer: Contamination — the repository, the issue text, and often the fix are in the pretraining data, so recall is scored as reasoning. And environment fragility: flaky tests, network-dependent setup, and patches that pass the graded test while breaking behaviour the test does not cover.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does grading only the final answer under-measure a tool-using agent?
reviewQuestions.answer: It cannot distinguish a correct answer reached correctly from one reached after ten wasted calls, a destructive side effect, or a lucky guess with a broken tool. The trajectory carries the signal you act on: tool choice, argument validity, recovery from errors, and the verified end state.

reviewQuestions.question: How do you set a release gate on a stochastic system without either blocking every release or catching nothing?
reviewQuestions.answer: Run each frozen case n times and gate on a confidence interval around the aggregate, not a single run's exact output. Version the grader alongside the cases so a rubric change is a visible diff, and set the threshold from the observed run-to-run variance rather than picking a round number.

reviewQuestions.question: Name two mechanically different ways to detect a probable hallucination, and what each one misses.
reviewQuestions.answer: Consistency sampling: generate several times and measure disagreement — cheap, but a confidently wrong model agrees with itself. Grounding checks: require each claim to map to a retrieved span — strong for factual claims, but useless where no evidence was retrievable and blind to reasoning errors.

reviewQuestions.question: What identifier makes agent traces useful, and what breaks without it?
reviewQuestions.answer: A run id propagated to every step, model call, and tool invocation, with each step carrying its parent. Without it you have a pile of independent LLM calls and no way to reconstruct why the agent did something, attribute cost to an outcome, or find the step where a run went wrong.

reviewQuestions.question: What must be captured for an agent run to be replayable, and which dependency is usually missed?
reviewQuestions.answer: Prompt version, model version and sampling parameters, the full context sent, every tool result, and each state transition.
