The usually-missed one is tool output: replaying against a live API returns different data, so the run diverges and you are debugging a new run, not the one that failed.

reviewQuestions.question: What separates evidence from an assertion when an agent reports "the tests pass"?
reviewQuestions.answer: Evidence is independently checkable without trusting the agent: the command run, its exit code, the captured output, the diff applied. "Tests pass" is a claim the model generated, which it can produce whether or not it ran anything. Each acceptance criterion needs an artifact a reviewer can re-inspect.

reviewQuestions.question: Review capacity is finite. What decides which cases reach a human, and what do you measure about the reviewers themselves?
reviewQuestions.answer: Route by expected cost of being wrong — model uncertainty times blast radius — not by a flat sample rate. Measure inter-reviewer agreement: if two reviewers disagree on the same case, the rubric is ambiguous and their labels cannot be trusted as ground truth for evals.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is "config A is better than config B" usually an unanswerable question?
reviewQuestions.answer: Because it is multi-objective. A can win on quality while losing on p95 latency and cost per request, and the ranking flips with traffic mix. The honest output is a Pareto frontier measured on one representative workload, plus an explicit statement of the budget that picks a point on it.

reviewQuestions.question: What makes a review comment actionable rather than noise?
reviewQuestions.answer: It names the behaviour that changes, the condition that triggers it, and a concrete remediation — not a preference. Style belongs to the formatter and the linter; spending reviewer attention there crowds out the correctness and blast-radius questions only a human reading the intent can raise.

reviewQuestions.question: Static analysis has false positives and dynamic analysis has false negatives. Explain why each is structural, not a tool defect.
reviewQuestions.answer: Static analysis over-approximates the set of possible executions, so it flags paths that can never actually run. Dynamic analysis observes only the executions you triggered, so any bug on an unexercised path is invisible. Neither is fixable by a better tool — it follows from what each one reasons about.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is a flaky test worse than a failing one?
reviewQuestions.answer: A failing test carries information and blocks the bad change. A flaky one trains everyone to re-run until green, which is the same as deleting every test in the suite from a signal standpoint. That is why flakes get quarantined and fixed as defects rather than retried.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is stable symbol identity the hard part of a codebase graph, rather than parsing?
reviewQuestions.answer: Edges are only useful if the same symbol keeps the same identity across commits, files, and languages — otherwise a rename looks like a delete plus an add and every historical edge breaks. Parsing gives you a syntax tree; resolving that tree to durable, cross-repository identifiers is the work.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is the static dependency graph an upper bound on blast radius, and what narrows it?
reviewQuestions.answer: It lists everything that could be affected, including dead code and paths never executed in production. Runtime evidence — traces, coverage, actual callers — narrows it to what is really reachable, and public-contract boundaries tell you where a change is observable versus internal.

reviewQuestions.question: What does the language-server architecture decouple, and what problem does that solve?
reviewQuestions.answer: Language intelligence from the editor. Before it, n languages times m editors meant n*m integrations; a shared JSON-RPC protocol makes it n+m. The cost is that everything crosses a process boundary, so incremental sync and cancellation matter more than raw analysis speed.

reviewQuestions.question: What makes an edit reversible in a coding agent, and why does that matter more than edit quality?
reviewQuestions.answer: Working in a branch or worktree with every change expressed as a diff, so any step can be inspected and dropped. It matters more because a wrong-but-reverted edit costs a retry, while an unreviewable pile of in-place mutations costs the human the whole diff — the handoff, not the model, is the bottleneck.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is embedding-based semantic search insufficient on its own for repository questions?
reviewQuestions.answer: Embeddings find text that reads similarly; most repository questions are structural — who calls this, what breaks if I change it, why was this written. Those need the symbol graph and the history. The two are complementary: retrieval finds candidates, the graph proves the relationship.

reviewQuestions.question: An SBOM and a provenance attestation answer different questions. What are they?
reviewQuestions.answer: The SBOM answers what is inside the artifact — the dependency inventory you scan for vulnerabilities. Provenance answers how the artifact was produced: which source commit, which builder, which inputs. You need both, because a correct ingredient list says nothing about who did the cooking.

reviewQuestions.question: Why must reproduction come before hypothesis generation in an automated repair loop?
reviewQuestions.answer: Without a failing case you cannot tell a fix from a coincidence — the loop has no oracle and will happily produce patches that satisfy the model's story. A deterministic reproducer also lets delta debugging shrink the input, which narrows the causal surface far faster than reasoning about the whole program.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does backgrounding matter more on mobile than on web, and what does it force into the architecture?
reviewQuestions.answer: The OS can suspend or kill a backgrounded app at any moment with no warning and no unload hook. So in-memory state is not durable, timers stop, and sockets die. Anything the user would notice losing must be persisted at each step, and reconnect-and-resync has to be a normal path, not an error path.

reviewQuestions.question: Which interaction states are routinely missing from a design, and why do they cause the most support load?
reviewQuestions.answer: Empty, loading, partial, error, and offline. Designs get built around the populated happy path, so those states are invented by whoever implements them — inconsistently. They are also the states a user is in exactly when they are already stuck, which is when an unclear screen becomes a support ticket.

reviewQuestions.question: Optimistic UI applies the change locally before the server confirms. What has to be designed for that not to corrupt state?
reviewQuestions.answer: A rollback path and an ordering rule. Each local mutation is held pending with an id; the server response either confirms or reverses it, and concurrent remote updates must be reconciled against the pending set rather than blindly overwriting. Without that, a rejected write leaves the UI showing something that never happened.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is simulation usually stepped at a fixed timestep while rendering runs as fast as it can?
reviewQuestions.answer: Physics integrated with a variable dt is not reproducible and blows up at frame spikes; a fixed step makes it deterministic. Rendering then interpolates between the last two simulation states to match the display's refresh, which is why the loop accumulates time and runs zero or more fixed steps per frame.

reviewQuestions.question: What does a projector do in a vision-language model, and why is aligned data the bottleneck?
reviewQuestions.answer: It maps the vision encoder's output into the language model's token embedding space so images arrive as pseudo-tokens. The bottleneck is paired data: the alignment is learned from image-text pairs, and their coverage and caption quality decide what the model can actually refer to, not the encoder's strength.

reviewQuestions.question: Why do CNNs still often beat vision transformers on small datasets?
reviewQuestions.answer: Convolutions build in locality and translation equivariance, so the model starts with a correct prior about images. A ViT has to learn that from data, which is why it needs large-scale pretraining or heavy augmentation to catch up — and why it overtakes the CNN once that data exists.

reviewQuestions.question: Per-frame landmark detection is accurate but the skeleton jitters. What is happening and what is the tradeoff in fixing it?
reviewQuestions.answer: Independent per-frame estimates carry independent noise, so the output jitters even when each frame is close. Temporal filtering or a motion prior smooths it — at the cost of lag: the more smoothing, the later the tracker follows a genuine fast movement. That is the latency-versus-stability knob.

reviewQuestions.question: What is endpointing, and why does it dominate perceived latency in a voice agent?
reviewQuestions.answer: Deciding the user has finished speaking. Every stage after it is measurable, but the endpointer's silence threshold is dead time added to every turn — set it short and you interrupt people mid-sentence, long and the agent feels slow. It is the one latency component you cannot optimise away with faster models.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is temporal consistency harder in video generation than image quality?
reviewQuestions.answer: Each frame is individually plausible while the sequence is not — identity, lighting, and geometry drift because nothing ties frame t to frame t-1. Fixing it means conditioning across frames (3D attention, latent propagation), which raises cost superlinearly with length, and human eyes detect flicker far below the threshold for spatial artefacts.

reviewQuestions.question: What is the sim-to-real gap, and what is the standard way of closing it?
reviewQuestions.answer: A policy trained in simulation fails on hardware because contact dynamics, friction, sensor noise, and latency are all approximated. Domain randomisation is the standard answer: randomise those parameters during training so the policy must be robust across them rather than fitted to one wrong physics model.

reviewQuestions.question: An anchor drifts, so placed content slowly slides off the real surface. What causes it and what does the UI owe the user?
reviewQuestions.answer: Tracking accumulates error, and relocalisation corrects it in a jump when a known feature is re-observed. The interface owes visible tracking confidence, content that re-anchors to a recognised plane instead of a raw pose, and a recovery path when the anchor is lost rather than silently misplaced content.

reviewQuestions.question: What does Fitts's law predict, and what design rule follows from it?
reviewQuestions.answer: Time to hit a target grows with distance and shrinks with target size, logarithmically. So make frequent targets large and close to where the cursor or thumb already is — and note that screen edges are effectively infinite in size, which is why edge and corner placement is disproportionately fast.

reviewQuestions.question: A dynamic array's push is O(1) amortised, yet one push can still take O(n). What does the amortised bound actually promise, and when is it the wrong bound to quote?
reviewQuestions.answer: It promises that any sequence of n pushes costs O(n) in total, because the doubling copies form a geometric series — not that any single push is cheap. It is the wrong bound when a single call has a deadline: a latency budget, a real-time frame, or a request p99, where the rare O(n) copy is exactly the case that hurts.

reviewQuestions.question: You sort records by score, then by date, expecting both orderings to hold. Why does this only work if the sort is stable, and what breaks if it is not?
reviewQuestions.answer: Sorting by date first and score second only preserves the date order within equal scores if equal elements keep their relative positions — that is stability. Without it the second pass may reorder ties arbitrarily, so records with the same score come back in an unpredictable date order. The fix is either a stable sort or a single comparator that ranks on score then date explicitly.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is a back-of-the-envelope estimate useful even when the inputs are guesses, and what makes an estimate that is wrong by 10x different from one wrong by 2x?
reviewQuestions.answer: The estimate exists to eliminate architectures, not to predict a bill. Being 2x out changes nothing — the same storage engine and shard count still apply. Being 10x out crosses a boundary: single machine to fleet, one region to many, cron to queue. So carry one significant figure, size for peak rather than mean, and include the multipliers that actually dominate — replication, indexes, retention.

reviewQuestions.question: Two requirements: 'users can follow each other' and 'reads outnumber writes 100 to 1'. Which one changes the architecture, and why is that the whole point of the split?
reviewQuestions.answer: The read/write ratio does. 'Users can follow each other' is satisfiable by almost any design, so it constrains nothing; a 100:1 read skew immediately argues for caching, read replicas, and probably fan-out on write. Functional requirements tell you what to build, non-functional ones tell you what it has to survive — and only the second kind can rule a design out, which is why they are worth extracting first.

reviewQuestions.question: Prefix sums answer range-sum in O(1). Why does the same trick fail for range-minimum, and what does that tell you about which operations it works for?
reviewQuestions.answer: Because the query is a subtraction: sum(i..j) = prefix[j+1] - prefix[i] only recovers the range if the operation can be undone. Addition is invertible, min is not — knowing the min over 0..j and over 0..i tells you nothing about the min between them. So prefix works for associative AND invertible operations (sum, xor, product over a field); for min or max you need a structure that recomputes over overlapping blocks, like a sparse table.

reviewQuestions.question: A monotonic stack has a while loop nested inside a for loop, yet it runs in O(n). What is the counting argument, and at which moment is an element's answer known?
reviewQuestions.answer: Each index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once, so the inner while performs at most n pops across the entire outer loop — the total work is bounded by pushes, not by the nesting. The answer is known at the moment of the pop: the element being popped has just met the first element to its right that is greater, which is precisely its next-greater. Anything still on the stack when the scan ends never met one.

reviewQuestions.question: Rabin-Karp finds a window whose hash equals the pattern's hash. Why is it wrong to report a match, and what is the worst case if you skip the check?
reviewQuestions.answer: Equal hashes mean the window might match — hashing maps many strings to one value, so a collision is a false positive. Reporting without comparing characters returns wrong answers on ordinary input and can be induced deliberately: an adversary who knows your modulus can force a collision on every window, which also drags the runtime to O(nm) since you would be verifying everywhere. The verification is what keeps it correct; a large random-ish modulus is what keeps it fast.

reviewQuestions.question: Someone proposes routing traffic along the MST because it is the cheapest set of edges. What is wrong with that reasoning?
reviewQuestions.answer: An MST minimises the total weight of the edge set, not the distance between any particular pair. The unique MST path between two nodes can be arbitrarily worse than their shortest path — a direct cheap-ish edge is excluded whenever it would form a cycle, even though it is the best route. Minimum total cost and minimum pairwise distance are different objectives; the second needs Dijkstra or Floyd-Warshall.

reviewQuestions.question: Two on-call engineers each check 'is anyone else on duty?', both see one other person, and both go off duty. Snapshot isolation did not stop it. Why not, and what does?
reviewQuestions.answer: Both transactions read the same consistent snapshot and then wrote DIFFERENT rows — their own. Snapshot isolation only rejects transactions that write the same row, so disjoint writes over an overlapping read set slip through; this is write skew. The invariant spanned rows neither transaction wrote. Fixes: true serializable isolation, a materialised lock via SELECT FOR UPDATE on the rows read, or a constraint that expresses the invariant in the database rather than in the transaction.

reviewQuestions.question: A query was fast in staging and unusable in production with the same plan shape. Why do cardinality estimates explain this more often than the join algorithm itself?
reviewQuestions.answer: The planner chooses the algorithm from estimated row counts. Staging has small, freshly-analysed tables, so the estimate is close and a nested loop over a few hundred rows is genuinely best. In production the same estimate can be off by orders of magnitude — stale statistics, skew, or a correlated predicate the planner assumes is independent — and that nested loop now runs millions of index probes where a hash join would have been linear. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows estimated against actual rows, which is where the discrepancy becomes visible.

reviewQuestions.question: A dependency slows down, clients retry three times at each of three layers, and the outage gets worse. Trace the amplification and name the two mechanisms that stop it.
reviewQuestions.answer: Three retries at three layers multiply, not add: one user request becomes up to 27 at the bottom, and every client retrying on the same schedule lands simultaneously — load rises exactly when the dependency has least capacity. Jittered exponential backoff spreads the arrivals in time so the herd desynchronises; a circuit breaker stops them entirely once failures pass a threshold, failing fast to give the dependency room to recover. A retry budget is the third lever: cap retries as a fraction of total traffic, and retry at ONE layer, not every layer.

reviewQuestions.question: A reviewer says 'we set CORS headers, so the API is protected from other sites.' Why is that backwards, and what actually defends the endpoint?
reviewQuestions.answer: CORS relaxes the same-origin policy rather than enforcing it — a CORS header grants a foreign origin access that the browser would otherwise deny, so a permissive one removes protection. It also only constrains browsers; curl and any server ignore it entirely. What defends the endpoint is authentication and authorisation checked server-side on every request, plus a CSRF token or SameSite cookies for state-changing requests the browser would otherwise authenticate automatically.

reviewQuestions.question: A service sits at 70% CPU and someone reports '30% headroom'. Using the utilisation curve, why is that reading wrong?
reviewQuestions.answer: Headroom is not linear in utilisation. Queueing delay scales as 1/(1−ρ), so at ρ=0.7 the wait is already about 2.3x the service time, and the remaining 30% of capacity buys far less than the first 30% did — pushing to 0.9 triples the wait again. Capacity is consumed smoothly but latency is not, which is why systems degrade long before saturation and why utilisation targets sit well below 100%.

reviewQuestions.question: In high dimensions the ratio (farthest − nearest)/nearest tends to zero. What does that break, and why do vector databases still work?
reviewQuestions.answer: It breaks pruning. An index that discards candidates because they are 'too far' needs the distances to differ meaningfully; once nearest and farthest converge, there is nothing to discard and exact search degenerates to a full scan. Vector databases still work because the theorem assumes independent uniformly distributed coordinates, and real embeddings do not look like that — they concentrate on a much lower-dimensional manifold, leaving enough structure for graph and partition indexes to exploit.

reviewQuestions.question: WAND skips documents without scoring them. Why is the returned top-k still exactly the same as an exhaustive scan, and when does the technique stop paying off?
reviewQuestions.answer: Because a document is only skipped when the SUM OF UPPER BOUNDS on its matching terms cannot exceed the current k-th best score — the skip is justified by a bound on the best case, so no skipped document could have entered the top k. The win shrinks as k grows: a larger k keeps the threshold lower for longer, so fewer documents fall under it, and it vanishes entirely for queries that need deep result sets rather than a shallow top-k.

reviewQuestions.question: A fixed-window limiter allows 100 requests per minute, yet a client sustains 200 in a sixty-second span. Explain the mechanism and what fixes it.
reviewQuestions.answer: The client sends 100 in the last instant of one window and 100 in the first instant of the next. Each window is individually within budget, but the sixty seconds straddling the boundary sees double the intended rate. A token bucket refills continuously so there is no boundary to exploit, and it makes the permitted burst explicit — the bucket capacity — rather than an accident of where the window happens to fall.

reviewQuestions.question: Switching a primary key from random UUIDv4 to UUIDv7 improved write throughput without any schema change. Why?
reviewQuestions.answer: UUIDv4 is random, so consecutive inserts land in unrelated positions of the B-tree: every insert dirties a different page, the working set becomes the whole index, and pages split repeatedly. UUIDv7 puts a millisecond timestamp in the high bits, so ids are roughly time-ordered and inserts concentrate at the right edge of the index — the same few pages stay hot in the buffer pool and splits become rare. Same uniqueness guarantee, very different locality.

reviewQuestions.question: You are three levels deep tracing a recursive call and have lost the thread. What is the argument that makes tracing unnecessary, and what must you check instead?
reviewQuestions.answer: Induction. You assume the recursive call is already correct on a smaller input and only verify that the step combining its result is correct — the call tree takes care of itself. What you must actually check is that every path reaches a base case and that the input strictly shrinks on every call; those two together are what the induction rests on, and they are also the only places termination bugs live.

reviewQuestions.question: Quickselect is O(n) and quicksort is O(n log n) despite the same partition step. Where does the log factor go, and why is the O(n) only expected?
reviewQuestions.answer: Quicksort recurses into both partitions, so every level does n work and there are log n levels. Quickselect knows which partition contains the k-th element and discards the other, so the work is n + n/2 + n/4 … which is a geometric series summing to 2n. It is only expected because the halving depends on the pivot landing near the middle; a bad pivot on adversarial or sorted input shrinks the problem by one element at a time and gives O(n²). Randomised pivots or median-of-medians restore the guarantee.

reviewQuestions.question: When is denormalising a schema a legitimate engineering decision rather than a shortcut, and what must you own if you do it?
reviewQuestions.answer: It is legitimate when reads dominate by a wide margin, the join is measurably the bottleneck, and the duplicated value changes rarely. What you take on is the write path: every copy now needs a mechanism that updates it — a trigger, an application invariant, or a rebuild job — because the anomaly normalisation was preventing has not gone away, you have merely accepted responsibility for it. Duplication with no owner is how two rows end up disagreeing about the same fact.

reviewQuestions.question: A nightly report scans a large table and the morning cache hit rate collapses. What did plain LRU do, and how does LRU-K prevent it?
reviewQuestions.answer: The scan touched every page exactly once. Under LRU each of those pages was the most-recently-used at the moment it was read, so they evicted the genuinely hot working set — which is then cold at 9am. LRU-K only promotes a page into the resident set on its K-th access, so single-touch scan pages stay in a probationary tier and are evicted before anything seen twice. The hot set survives because the policy distinguishes 'recent' from 'repeatedly useful'.

reviewQuestions.question: An endpoint using OFFSET is fine on page 1 and times out on page 5,000, and users occasionally report a duplicated row. Explain both symptoms and the single change that fixes them.
reviewQuestions.answer: OFFSET makes the database generate and discard every skipped row, so cost grows linearly with page depth — page 5,000 produces 100,000 rows to return 20. The duplicate is the same mechanism seen differently: a row inserted before the window shifts everything down by one, so the next page re-serves an item the client already had. Keyset pagination fixes both by resuming after a key rather than counting skipped rows: each page is an index seek at constant cost, and an insert elsewhere cannot move the window.

reviewQuestions.question: 'At least one collision among k hashed items' is awkward to count directly. What is the standard move, and why is it easier?
reviewQuestions.answer: Count the complement — the probability that ALL k are distinct — and subtract from 1. 'At least one' is a union over many overlapping events, so direct counting needs inclusion-exclusion across every subset; 'all distinct' is a single product of independent-ish factors. This is the birthday-paradox calculation, and it is why collisions appear at roughly sqrt(N) items rather than N.

reviewQuestions.question: Subtracting two nearly equal floats is called catastrophic. What exactly is lost, and why does using doubles only postpone it?
reviewQuestions.answer: Floating point keeps a fixed number of significant digits, so when two close numbers are subtracted the leading digits — the ones that agreed — cancel and the result is carried by the trailing digits, which are precisely the least accurate. Relative error explodes even though absolute error did not change. Doubles give more significant digits, so the failure needs closer inputs, but the mechanism is identical. The real fix is algebraic: reorder to avoid the subtraction, or shift domains as log-sum-exp does.

reviewQuestions.question: NDCG has zero gradient almost everywhere. How does LambdaMART optimise it anyway?
reviewQuestions.answer: NDCG depends only on sort order, so an infinitesimal score change usually moves nothing and the derivative is zero — until a swap happens, where it jumps. LambdaMART never differentiates NDCG. It computes a pairwise gradient for each document pair and scales it by |ΔNDCG|, the change that swapping those two would cause. The metric enters as a weight rather than as a function to differentiate, so pairs that matter to NDCG pull harder.

reviewQuestions.question: A team trains its ranker on click-through rate and the ranking gets more entrenched each cycle. Explain the loop and the standard correction.
reviewQuestions.answer: A click requires the user to have examined the result, and examination falls steeply with rank — so CTR measures relevance multiplied by position. Training on it teaches the model that being at the top predicts clicks, it promotes what was already promoted, and the next log is even more skewed. Inverse-propensity weighting corrects it by dividing each click by the estimated examination probability for that position, so a click from rank 8 counts far more than one from rank 1. Estimating those propensities honestly needs some randomisation in the logging policy.

reviewQuestions.question: Binary quantisation cuts memory 32x but loses a lot of precision. Why does the two-stage retrieve-then-rescore pattern get most of the accuracy back?
reviewQuestions.answer: The compressed representation only has to be good enough to RANK candidates roughly — to get the true nearest neighbours somewhere into an over-fetched candidate set of, say, 10x k. Precision is then restored by rescoring just those few hundred candidates against full-precision vectors, which is cheap because it touches a tiny fraction of the index. You pay full precision only where it changes the answer, so memory follows the compressed vectors and accuracy follows the rescore.

reviewQuestions.question: Moving an ANN index from RAM to SSD inverts what you optimise. What becomes the cost, and how does DiskANN keep it low?
reviewQuestions.answer: In memory the cost is distance comparisons; on SSD it is random reads, each around 100 microseconds — thousands of times a comparison. A traversal that was cheap becomes dominated by the number of pages touched, so optimising comparison count is optimising the wrong term. DiskANN keeps compressed vectors resident in RAM to steer the search and reads full-precision neighbourhoods from SSD only for the few nodes it actually needs, turning a long traversal into a handful of reads.

reviewQuestions.question: Why can a proximity-graph index not simply remove a deleted node, and what does the tombstone cost you over time?
reviewQuestions.answer: Other nodes reach their neighbours through that node's edges; excising it can disconnect regions of the graph and silently reduce recall for queries that used to route through it. So implementations mark it deleted and filter it from results. The debt is that the node still occupies memory and is still traversed, consuming search budget that returns nothing — as the tombstone ratio climbs, recall and latency both drift with no code change, until a compaction rebuilds the region.

reviewQuestions.question: Why do content-hashed URLs with a one-year TTL beat a short TTL plus purge-on-deploy?
reviewQuestions.answer: Because they make invalidation unnecessary rather than fast. A hashed URL names a specific byte sequence, so a change produces a different URL — the old entry is never wrong, it is simply unreferenced, and the new one is a plain cache miss. Purge is eventually consistent across POPs, can fail partially, and leaves a window where users get stale content; a short TTL trades constant origin load for a smaller version of the same window. The immutable approach has neither problem.
